## [0.28.0] - 2026-11-18

### Security

- **A launch.json preLaunchTask and a lone C# file ask before running a folder's code.** A configuration's
  `preLaunchTask` ran its `.vscode/tasks.json` command in an untrusted folder with no question, and debugging a C#
  file outside any project built it there although the SDK's build imports the folders' `Directory.Build.props` and
  `.targets`. Both now ask for workspace trust first, as Make, CMake and dotnet projects do; declining runs nothing.
- **Mill and sbt builds ask before running a folder's code.** A cloned repository's own `./mill` launcher ran on the
  first build with no question, unlike `./mvnw` and `./gradlew`. Mill and sbt builds now ask for workspace trust the
  way Maven and Gradle do, on a repository launcher or your own `mill`/`sbt` alike, since `build.mill`, `build.sc`,
  `build.sbt` and `project/` are Scala code the build compiles and runs. The question lists the launcher, the build
  scripts, a `mill-build/` meta-build and the launcher options files (`.mill-jvm-opts`, `.jvmopts`, `.sbtopts`).
  Running a task, Run on a Scala file of the build, Test Results, Run and Debug's build before a launch and Load all
  tasks all ask; declining runs nothing. A folder you already trusted is unchanged.
- **Leiningen, Babashka, Clojure CLI, Cargo, Scala CLI and npm builds ask before running a folder's code.** Each
  of these runs code the repository supplies beyond the task you pick: Leiningen evaluates `project.clj` and its
  plugins, Babashka runs a task's `:init` and `:depends` first, a `deps.edn` alias can add JVM options such as a
  `-javaagent`, Cargo compiles and runs `build.rs` scripts and procedural macros, Scala CLI runs macros and compiler
  plugins as it compiles, and npm runs `pre` and `post` scripts, install hooks and, through a `.yarnrc.yml`
  `yarnPath`, a yarn the repository ships. Their first build in a folder now asks for workspace trust, as Maven,
  Gradle, sbt and Mill do, listing what it found (`.cargo/config.toml`, `rust-toolchain.toml`, `.npmrc`,
  `.yarnrc.yml`, `.pnpmfile.cjs`, `.lein-classpath` and the like); declining runs nothing. Go builds are not asked
  about: `go build` never runs a module's code. A folder you already trusted is unchanged.
- **Run and Debug ask the same question before loading a project.** Run on a Clojure file of a Leiningen,
  `deps.edn` or `bb.edn` project started `lein`, `clojure` or `bb` there without asking, and so did a file of a Scala
  CLI project (`project.scala`) and an npm run configuration, though the build tool's own window asked for the same
  folder. Run and Debug on such a file or configuration now ask for that tool's workspace trust first; declining
  runs nothing, and Rerun asks again if you revoked trust since. A file run on its own, in no project, is not asked
  about.

### Added

- **Every setting can be changed from the Command Palette.** Settings that were only rows of the Settings window
  now have commands too (SET-06, Pauta 6.0.1). Most pages have one that lists their settings by name with their
  values and flips the one you pick, lists its choices or asks for its value: Terminal: Change a Setting… (the
  shell, theme, text size, cursor, desktop notifications and the rest), Debug: Change a Setting…, LSP: Change a
  Language Setting… (ShellCheck and shfmt, XML and HTML formatting, ESLint and the formatters, the actions on
  save), Build: Change a Setting… (each build tool's command, Maven's default JDK, Node.js, Build before Run),
  Encryption: Change a Setting…, Settings Sync: Change a Setting…, Web: Change a Setting… and Editor: Change a
  PDF Setting…. New single commands: View: Toggle a File Preview…, View: Toggle Word Wrap in Prose, View: Toggle Quick Fix Lightbulb, View: Toggle Problem Counter,
  GitHub: Set gh Command…, Remote: Set Container Engine…, Spell Check: Set Default Language…, AI: Set API Key…
  (typed into a field of dots), AI Agent: Set a Client's Command… and Markdown Lint: Set Rule Severity…. Each
  keeps what its Settings row would keep and shows in an open Settings window at once. The question before a
  paste of several lines into a terminal gets no command: it protects you, so only its row turns it off.
- **Debug Bash scripts.** Press Debug on a Bash script to stop at its breakpoints, step through it and read its
  variables in a watch or by hovering (`total`, or `$total` as the script writes it). Install Bash Debug from
  Settings → Debugging → Bash; it brings its own bashdb and runs on Node.js. Scripts of other shells (zsh, fish) still
  point at Run with Trace.
- **Debug Test at Caret in C#.** In an xUnit, NUnit or MSTest project, Debug Test at Caret runs the test the caret
  is in (or every test of its class) under `dotnet test` and attaches the debugger to it, so its breakpoints stop with
  the test's values. Stop ends the run; Restart runs the same test again.
- **Breakpoints in Django and Jinja templates.** A breakpoint on a line of a Django or Jinja template stops there,
  with the template's variables (the context, a loop's item and `forloop`) in the Debug window. Editora turns it on for
  a project that uses Django (a `manage.py`, or Django in its requirements) or Jinja (Jinja2 or Flask in its
  requirements); Settings → Debugging → Python → Template breakpoints can turn it on or off for every project. Before,
  a Django template's breakpoint was never hit, and a Jinja one stopped at the wrong place.
- **Go goroutines your way in the Threads view.** A Go program's runtime goroutines (the garbage collector's
  workers, the finalizer) are left out of the Threads view, and a goroutine started under pprof labels shows them in
  its name (`[Go 20 job:resize-0] main.worker`). Right-click the Threads view to show the runtime's goroutines again or
  to filter them with Delve's own filter (`-with label job=*`); the change applies to the running program at once and
  is kept. Settings → Debugging → Go goroutines holds all three.
- **Show Value As.** Right-click a number in the Variables view or a watch and choose Show Value As ▸ Decimal,
  Hexadecimal, Binary, Octal or Character to see that one value that way, while the others stay as they are. A
  negative number shows as its two's complement for its type (`-42` as an `int` is `0xffffffd6`), a `char` shows its
  code, and choosing it on an array or object shows all the numbers in it that way. The choice stays at the next stop
  and in the next session until the window closes, and Copy Value copies what you see. It works with every debugger,
  including those that ignore Show Numbers as Hexadecimal (CodeLLDB, Delve, js-debug).
- **A copy button on the Markdown preview's code blocks.** Point at a code block in the preview and a copy button
  shows in its top right corner, beside the language; one click copies the block's code, and a check mark says it
  worked. Fenced and indented blocks both have it; hover and completion popups do not.
- **Set Value on a watch.** Right-click a watch while the program is paused and choose Set Value… to give its
  expression a new value — a variable, a field, an element — as IntelliJ and Visual Studio allow. Python and
  JavaScript set the expression directly; Java, Go and C/C++ set the variable a watch names, or (Java) evaluate the
  assignment. The other watches are evaluated again at once.
- **An evaluation time limit.** A watch, a Debug console line or a hover that calls a function which never returns
  no longer holds the paused program for good: with GDB and Python's debugger, the call is stopped after the time
  limit (10 s by default, Settings → Debugging → Evaluating expressions), the program stays paused on the same line,
  and the next expression is evaluated there. CodeLLDB already stops such a call in a watch or hover by itself; Java,
  JavaScript and Go have no limit to set, and Editora still stops waiting after 30 s and says the program is still
  running the expression.
- **Undo Last Removal.** Some things you make are removed with one key and no question, because a question each time
  would be tiresome: a watch, a breakpoint that has a condition, a log message, a hit count, a group or a filter, a
  method breakpoint or field watchpoint with a condition, an exception breakpoint, a value pinned to a line or all of
  a line's, a bookmark with a mnemonic, a key binding you removed or reset, a word of your personal dictionary, a
  setting put back to its default and a project's value taken off a setting. Each of these now tells you so in the
  status bar, and Edit: Undo Last Removal (Edit menu and Command Palette; it has no key until you give it one) puts
  the last one back as it was: in its place in the list, with its condition, its paused state or its mnemonic. It
  keeps the twenty newest removals of a window, until the window closes. When what was removed can no longer go back
  where it was (the file was closed, the line reads something else, the key runs another command now, a new breakpoint
  is on the line), it says so and changes nothing. A plain breakpoint or bookmark is not recorded: the key that
  removed it sets it again. A removal made in Settings is said in the editor window's status bar and is undone from
  the editor window.
- **Don't step into.** Name the code Step Into should go over — a class or package (`com.shop.util.*`), a module
  (`requests`), a function (`fmt.*`, `std::*`) or a file (`**/vendor/**`) — in Settings → Debugging, or right-click a
  frame in the call stack and choose Don't Step Into This…, which offers its class, file, package or namespace. Java,
  Python, JavaScript and the other JVM languages' debuggers skip it themselves; with Go, Rust, C/C++ and the rest,
  Editora steps back out when a step lands there. A breakpoint inside it still stops.
- **View as DataFrame and View as Array.** A pandas DataFrame or Series, or a numpy array, in a program you are
  debugging opens as a table of its rows, as PyCharm's data viewer does: right-click it in Variables, a watch or an
  evaluate result. The columns are named as in the data and show their dtype on hover, an array of more than two
  dimensions is laid out as rows of its last one, and Load More brings the next 1,000 rows. Filter, sort, Copy and
  Open as CSV work as in View as Table.
- **Exception breakpoints by type and condition.** Stop only when an exception of a type you name is thrown, as
  IntelliJ's exception breakpoints do: Debug: Add Exception Breakpoint… (offering the type of the exception the
  debugger is stopped on), or the new rows of Debug: Exception Breakpoints…. A type can be a pattern
  (`java.io.*`, `*Error`, `!InterruptedException`), and an optional condition is evaluated where the exception was
  thrown, so `KeyError` with `order.id == 42` stops on that one order's error and lets the rest go by. They are
  kept per project and work with every language whose debugger stops on exceptions. Checked with Python and Java.
- **The right-click rows of the Project tree, the Git windows and the Debug window are commands.** What they do can
  now be run from the Command Palette, and given a key, on the selected row: in the Project tree (and on the Project
  Map's rows) Rename, Delete, Stage, Revert, Compare with Branch, Show Git History, Find in Folder and the rest of the
  file menu; in the Commit window Open, Show Diff, Discard, Resolve and Accept Ours / Theirs; in the Git Log the
  changed files' rows; in the GitHub window Open on GitHub, Check Out and Review a pull request and View Failure Log;
  in Local History Restore and Label a version; in Bookmarks, Personal Notes and Test Results every row of their
  menus; and in the Debug window every row of the Variables, Threads, call stack and console menus. A row shows the
  key of its command when it has one. Run with nothing selected, or on a row its menu would not offer it for, a
  command says so in the status bar and does nothing; Delete, Revert and Discard still ask first.
- **Every right-click row and button of the Project Map is a command.** The ⋯ menu's options (Compact rows, Follow
  the debugger, the four flow directions and the rest), Project Overview, Dependencies, Code Metrics, Review Changes,
  Collapse All and Export; the filters, Clear, the zoom bar and the search results' arrows and list; a column's Show
  hidden, lock and Close; the rows of the map's menu and of a declaration's (Preview, Related Test / Subject, Show
  Callers as Cards, Symbol Graph, the In the Editor rows, Declaration History…); a card's menu, Open, find bar,
  gutter marks and Go to Line ×; and the bars and menus of the Dependencies, Code Metrics, Symbol Graph, History and
  Changes cards. Each acts on what the Map's keyboard is on: the selected row, the card, the place in a card. Working
  sets, trails, the breadcrumb's places and the open cards are picked from a list. Where the row or button would do
  nothing, the Map's status line says why.
- **Every other right-click row and button is a command too.** The rest of the panels' rows and buttons can now be run
  from the Command Palette, and given a key: the terminal's menu (Copy, Paste, Select All, Clear Scrollback, Copy Last
  Command Output, New Terminal Here, the link rows, Close Other Terminals, Reconnect); the Markdown preview's Copy All,
  Go to Source, Enlarge, Copy Link and Copy Code (for what the preview's selection is in); the HTTP panel's Save
  Response, Clear, Wrap, header copies, Run Again and Go to Request; the Markdown Lint, CSV, Doctor, TODO, Structure and
  Problems rows; the diff's whitespace, words, context, wrap and apply buttons and gutter arrows; the merge view's
  Accept and Save; the find bars' Match Case, Regular Expression and Whole Word, and every search field's ✕; the
  debugger's value popup, Evaluate window, Thread Dump, Parallel Stacks, table window, exception card and Application
  Log; the encryption banners; the print preview's bar; and the Welcome page's links. Each acts on what the keyboard
  is in, or on what the window shows (the active tab, an open tool window); with nothing there the status bar says so.
  A plugin's editor menu row is now a command of its own. No default keys were added. Git: Stage All, from the palette
  or a key, now saves unsaved files and asks about leftover conflict markers first, as the Commit window's button did.
  The Settings window's buttons and links that act are commands too (Reset All, Restore Backup, a page's help, Install…
  on a card, Revoke All, the Sync page's buttons, a list's Add, the Keymaps page's Record / Reset / Remove, the Macros
  page's buttons), as are a panel's drop-downs (Structure: Sort By…, TODO: Group By…, GitHub: Filter by State…, HTTP:
  Show Response History…, Debug: Choose Thread…), Markdown: Set Heading Level…, CSV: Rename Focused Column and Debug:
  Quick Evaluate at Caret (Alt+click's), and the terminal's find bar answers Find Next / Previous and Match Case.
- **Commands for the editor menu's run and debug rows, the diff's line rows and the tab menu's last two rows.** Debug
  Current File, Debug Main Class at Caret, Debug Test Class at Caret, Add Expression at Caret to Watches, Stage,
  Unstage and Revert Line at Caret and Open Line at Caret in Editor in a diff, Local History: Show History of Current
  File and Git: Annotate Current File. A right-click in a diff now puts the caret on the line clicked, as in the editor.
- **The Git remotes and worktrees managers have a right-click menu, and their buttons are commands.** Add, Rename,
  Set URL, Prune and Remove a remote, and Add, Open, Prune and Remove a worktree are commands of their own: on the row
  selected in the manager while it is open, and on one picked from a list otherwise. The Stash list's Show Changes,
  Pop, Branch and Copy Name are commands that pick a stash, as Unstash and Drop Stash were.
- **The hex viewer, the unified diff and an unchanged line of a diff have a right-click menu.** Copy and Select All;
  Edit → Copy and Select All, and their keys, now act on such a view, and on a console (Run, Build, External Tools,
  Test Results, the HTTP response), when it has the keyboard, instead of on the editor behind it.
- **After a prefix key, the window lists the keys that can follow.** Press `C-x` in the Emacs keymap (or `Ctrl+K`
  in the VS Code one) and wait a moment: a card at the bottom of the window lists every key that can come next,
  with the command it runs, and for a key that leads further, such as `C-x v`, how many commands lie behind it.
  It follows the keymap in force and your own bindings, flows a long list into columns, and goes away as soon as
  the sequence runs or is cancelled. It never takes the keyboard: the next key does what it always did, and a
  sequence typed at speed never shows it.
- **Step Back and Reverse Continue in the debugger.** Where the program can run backward, the Debug window has Step
  Back (B) and Reverse Continue (Shift+C), also under Run → Stepping. For C and C++ on GDB (Settings → Debugging →
  C and C++ debugger), turn on **Record Execution** at a stop: GDB records the program from there, and Step Back goes
  back over a statement with the variables as they were, Reverse Continue back to the previous breakpoint or to where
  recording began. Recording slows the program a lot, so turn it on just before the part you want to replay. A
  debugger that steps back by itself (Delve or CodeLLDB on rr) is used as it is. Nothing to install for GDB.
- **Move between the editor and the tool windows from the keyboard, both ways, in every keymap.** *Window:
  Other* already cycled forward but was bound in the Emacs keymap only, and nothing went back. There is now
  *Window: Other, Reverse*, and both are bound everywhere: `C-x o` and `C-x S-o` in Emacs, Alt+Page Down and
  Alt+Page Up in the CUA, VS Code, Sublime and IntelliJ keymaps. Both are in the Window menu.
- **Parallel Stacks in the debugger.** Debug: Parallel Stacks draws every thread's call stack as one tree, as
  Visual Studio's Parallel Stacks window does: threads that went through the same calls share a box, and the box
  branches where they went different ways, so twenty workers waiting in one place are one box of twenty threads. The
  thread you are looking at is highlighted all the way up, a click on a frame opens its line, and Copy puts the tree
  on the clipboard as text. A running program is paused for a moment and goes on, as with Thread Dump. It is in Run →
  Debugger and in the Threads view's and call stack's menus. Checked with Python, Java and Go.
- **A find command for each console.** *Output: Find*, *Run: Find in Output*, *External Tools: Find in
  Output*, *Debug: Find in Console*, *Find in Test Output* and *Application Log: Find* are in the Command
  Palette and can be given a key under Settings → Keymaps. Each shows its panel and opens the find bar, and
  run again it goes to the next match. The Find key pressed inside a console still works as before.
- **View as Table in the debugger.** Right-click a list, array, slice, set or map in Variables or a watch and choose
  View as Table: each element is a row and each of its fields a column, as in IntelliJ and Visual Studio. Columns sort
  (numbers by value), a filter keeps the rows that mention some text, Copy puts the rows on the clipboard ready for a
  spreadsheet, and Open as CSV opens them in a CSV tab. The table keeps the values of the stop it was opened at;
  Refresh reads them again at the current stop. Large collections show their first 1,000 elements. Checked with
  Python, Java and Go.
- **Keyboard Shortcuts in the Help menu.** Help → Keyboard Shortcuts opens the list of every command's keys
  in Settings, where you can search it and change a key. It is in the Command Palette as *Keyboard Shortcuts*.
- **Focus Menu Bar.** *View: Focus Menu Bar* opens the first menu so the arrow keys can walk the menu bar.
  It is on F10 in the Emacs and IntelliJ keymaps and on Ctrl+Shift+F10 in the CUA, VS Code and Sublime
  keymaps, where F10 steps the debugger and the menu bar could not be reached from the keyboard at all.
- **Open Core Dump.** Run → Launch → Debug: Open Core Dump… opens the core file a crashed Go, C, C++ or Rust program
  left (or one `gcore` made) in the debugger, as GoLand and CLion do: the crashed thread's stack, shown at the program's
  own line rather than the runtime's, every other thread, and their variables, which you can evaluate and watch. On
  Linux the program is found in the core; otherwise Editora asks for it. Go cores open in Delve, the rest in CodeLLDB.
  A core cannot be run, so Continue and the steps are disabled and say why. A launch.json configuration that opens a
  core (Delve's `"mode": "core"`) gets the same treatment.
- **`--` on the command line.** Every argument after `--` is a file, so `editora -- -notes.txt` opens a file
  whose name starts with a dash, and a lone `-` is a file name too.
- **Breakpoint filters.** A breakpoint can now stop only in some threads (`worker-*`), only when called from some
  functions (`OrderService.save`), or only on one object, the one you marked with Mark Object, as IntelliJ's
  breakpoint filters do. Set them in Edit Breakpoint; patterns are separated by commas, `*` and `?` are wildcards and
  `!` excludes. Editora checks the filters at each stop and lets the program go on, unseen, when one fails, so they
  work with every language, and a filtered breakpoint's hit count and log message count only the hits that pass. Mark
  the object at the breakpoint's first stop, and the following stops are that object's.
- **A command for 44 buttons only the mouse could press.** Each is in the command palette, can be given a key
  under Settings → Keymaps, and the button's tooltip shows that key. On the Project Map: Back, Forward and
  History (the list of places the Map has been), Mouse and Keyboard Help, Options, and for the card the
  keyboard is in: Previous and Next Declaration in Card, Smaller and Larger Text in Card, Pin or Unpin Card,
  Show or Hide Card Structure, Show or Hide Card Notes and Close Card, plus Turn Hierarchy Around and Hide
  Trail Stop Note. Diff: Undo Last Applied Change, Save Result, Export as Patch and Leave Diff-Only Window.
  Git Log: Back to Branch Log, End Search and Refresh; GitHub: Refresh List; Local History: Back to the
  Current File. Debug: Add Evaluated Expression to Watches, Close Ended Session, and Previous and Next Page of
  Memory. Gradle, sbt and Mill: Load All Tasks. Test Results: Follow Newest Test Result and Show or Hide
  Passed, Failed and Skipped Tests. Also Agent: Open in Separate Window or Dock Back, Structure: Filter by
  Kind, Bookmarks and Notes: Show from All Projects, Markdown Lint: Most Severe First, Viewer: Previous Page,
  Next Page and Fit to Window for a PDF or an image, and Project: Choose a Project to Delete, which does from
  the keyboard what the trash on a row of the project dropdown does. A command with nothing to act on (no Map
  on screen, the keyboard not in a card, the tab not a PDF) says so in the status bar.
- **Type renderers in the debugger.** Choose how the debugger shows a value of a type, as IntelliJ's type renderers
  and Visual Studio's natvis do: a Money object as `12.50 EUR` rather than `Money@1f3a`, and its children as the fields
  or expressions that matter, with the debugger's own under [Raw View]. Right-click a value in Variables and choose
  Customize Rendering…, or manage them under Settings → Debugging → Type renderers. Expressions are the debugged
  language's, with `this` (or `self`) for the value. Renderers apply in Variables, watches, the Evaluate window and
  hover; a watch or evaluation that calls a method or assigns is not evaluated again. Mute Type Renderers, in the
  Variables menu, shows values as the debugger gives them. Checked with Java, Python and Go.
- **Buffer: Previous.** The tab before the selected one, wrapping to the last: the other way round from
  Buffer: Next, and beside it in the Window menu. Like Next it has no key of its own until you give it one
  under Settings → Keymaps.
- **Image, PDF and hex tabs are tabs like any other.** Their right-click menu has Close, Close Other Tabs,
  Close All Tabs, Close Unmodified Tabs, Close Tabs to the Left and to the Right, Reveal in Map, Reveal in
  File Manager, Open Terminal Here, Copy Path and Pin Tab. They can be pinned, and the pin is kept across a
  restart. Their tooltip is the file's full path. Reopen Closed Tab brings them back in the viewer they were
  in, so a text file you had opened as hex comes back as hex.
- **Every tab has the tab operations in its right-click menu.** A diff, a pull request review, a Markdown
  preview, a terminal moved to the editor, Welcome and Doctor had no menu or one row, Close. They now have
  Close, Close Other Tabs, Close All Tabs, Close Unmodified Tabs and Close Tabs to the Left and Right, after
  the rows of their own (a terminal's Rename and Move to Terminal Tool Window, a preview's lock).
- **A tab's tooltip names its file's Git status.** Under the path it says "Git: modified", "Git: untracked"
  and so on, so the title's color is not the only sign of it. Image, PDF and hex tabs are tinted by their
  file's Git status as editor tabs are.
- **Run configurations for C, C++, Go and Rust.** Run Configurations has four new types: C program, C++ program,
  Go program and Rust program (Cargo). Each names a source file, and that file is built the way Debug builds it: a C
  or C++ file's CMake or Make project, or the file alone with `cc` or `c++`; a Go file's package, or the file alone
  outside a module; a Rust file's Cargo package. Run then starts the program in the Run console, or a Terminal tab,
  and Debug starts it under CodeLLDB (GDB when that is the C and C++ debugger) or Delve. Both use the
  configuration's arguments, environment variables, working directory and before-launch step; a blank working
  directory is the folder Debug uses for the file. With such a file in front, Run Configurations → Add and Save as
  Run Configuration propose a configuration for it, where Add used to make a Java one. Until now these files could
  be debugged but not run. A Go or Rust test file runs or debugs all its tests. These configurations build and run on
  this computer only, not on a remote host, in a container or on a deployment. Run on a Go file of a package other
  than `main` says the file has no program to run, and builds nothing.
- **Thread Dump in the debugger.** Debug: Thread Dump, also in the Threads view's and the call stack's menus, shows
  every thread of the program with its call stack in a window of its own, as IntelliJ's Get Thread Dump does. Threads
  whose stacks are the same are merged into one row (twenty pool workers waiting in one place read as one), a filter
  finds a thread by its name or a frame, and a frame opens its code with Enter or a double-click, even after the
  program went on. On a running program it pauses for a moment, takes the dump and lets the program go on without
  moving the editor: the way to see what a program that hangs is doing. Copy puts the dump on the clipboard as text,
  Open as Text opens it in a read-only tab, and Take Again takes a new one. Works with Java, Python, Go and every
  other adapter that lists threads.
- **A zoom for the whole interface.** View → Zoom → Zoom In Interface, Zoom Out Interface and Reset
  Interface Zoom (also in the command palette, and as Interface zoom under Settings → Appearance) scale the
  menus, toolbar, tabs, tool windows, dialogs and status bar together, from 80% to 200% in steps of 10. It
  applies to every open window at once and is kept across launches. The editor's text keeps its own zoom
  (Ctrl/Cmd with =, - and 0), so the two can be set apart. Printed and exported pages are not affected,
  and the Print Preview window stays at 100%, the size its pages print at.
- **View → Zoom** gathers the text zoom's three commands, which had no menu row, with the interface zoom's.
- **Right-click menus in the References, Hierarchy, Find in Files and Undo History tool windows, the Message
  Log, the Application Log and the External Tools console.** A reference, a hierarchy item or a match has
  Open and Copy; an undo state has Restore This State; a message has Copy; the two logs have Select All and
  Copy, and the Application Log has Find in place of the stock Cut, Paste and Delete. The Menu key and
  Shift+F10 open each menu at the selected row.
- **Eight commands for those rows**, so the palette and a key binding of your own reach them: References: Open
  Reference and Copy Line, Hierarchy: Open Declaration and Copy Name, Find in Files: Open Match and Copy Line,
  Undo History: Restore This State, and Message Log: Copy. Each acts on the row selected in its panel.
- **The Copy key copies the selected row** in the References, Hierarchy and Find in Files trees: Ctrl+C (Cmd+C
  on macOS), or the Copy chord of the active keymap (M-w in Emacs).
- **Right-click menus on the lists that had none.** The lists on the Settings pages (Abbreviations, External
  Tools, Macros and their steps, Templates, Snippets, the personal dictionary and the spell-checked file types,
  Trusted Folders, the two toolbar lists, Remote sites, type renderers), the Project Map's Changes, History and
  Dependencies cards, its call stack, hierarchy and results columns and its trail editor, the debugger's Memory

  Recovery windows, the Backlinks tool window and a build tool's task tree now have one. Each holds what the list
  already did to a row through its buttons, a double-click or its keys (Open, Edit…, Connect, Deploy Now, Run,
  Play from Here, Rename…, Move Up and Down, Remove, Disable or Enable), and Copy where the row has text. The Menu
  key and Shift+F10 open it at the selected row.
- **Seven List commands for those rows**: List: Open, Copy, Rename…, Turn On or Off, Remove, Move Up and Move
  Down. Each does to the selected row of the list the keyboard is in what that list's menu row does, so the
  palette and a key binding of your own reach them, and says so on the status line when no list there can. A list
  in another window, such as Settings, is brought forward before the command acts in it. Three
  Project Map commands do the same for buttons of a card: Open Changed File in Editor, Compare Changed File, and
  Edit Trail Stop Note….
- **Settings…, Zen Mode, TODO and Bookmarks have menu rows** (Tools, View and Window), so no toolbar button is
  the only way to its action.
- **Five commands for buttons that had none**: Run: Run Selected Configuration and Debug: Debug Selected
  Configuration (the toolbar's buttons beside the configuration box, now also under Run → Debugger), Message Log:
  Clear, Output: Save Output… and Output: Show Previous Run.
- **Find in every console and in the Application Log.** The Run, External Tools and Debug consoles, the test
  output of Test Results and the Application Log window now have a find bar, as the build console did. Press
  your keymap's Find key in the view (the Application Log also has a Find button): it searches as you type and
  shows a count, Enter goes to the next match and Shift+Enter to the previous one, wrapping around, and Escape
  closes the bar and gives the keyboard back to the text.
- **Pauta conformance.** Editora now says which edition of [Pauta](https://pauta-project.dev/), the guidelines
  its family of apps follows, it is working toward and how far it has come. *Help → Pauta Conformance* (also in
  the Command Palette) lists every rule of Pauta 6.0.1 that Editora does not meet yet, each with one sentence on
  what is different and a link to the issue that tracks it; a rule's ID opens the rule, and *Copy as text* copies
  the list as Markdown. About gains *Working toward Pauta 6.0.1* and *Pauta conformance: Partial*, and its
  *Copy details* text carries both. The conformance is worked out from the list, so it cannot claim more than
  the list shows.
- **Debugger small wins: Copy as Expression, Jump to Type Source, Run to Here in the gutter, step timing and
  logpoint tokens.** *Copy as Expression* on a variable copies what gives its value in the stopped code, as the
  debugger itself names it (`items.get(0)` in Java, `d['k']` in Python, rather than `items[0]`); Add to Watches, Set
  Value and View As use it too. *Jump to Type Source* opens the class a value really has, which may be a subclass of
  the variable's type, in your code or the JDK's, through the language server. While the program is paused, hovering
  a line number turns it into an arrow: click it to run to that line, Shift+click to ignore the breakpoints on the
  way. After a step or Continue, the time the program ran appears faintly after the line it stopped on (*Show how
  long each step took* in Settings → Debug turns it off). A logpoint's message can use `$FUNCTION`, `$CALLER`,
  `$CALLSTACK`, `$TID` and `$TNAME` for the method, its caller, the call stack and the thread; such a logpoint
  pauses the program briefly at each hit while Editora writes the message.
- **Debug JavaScript in the browser.** *Debug in Browser…* opens a web page in Chrome, Edge or another Chromium
  browser (Chromium, Brave, Vivaldi) under the debugger, as VS Code does: breakpoints in the page's scripts stop it,
  with its variables, call stack, console output, stepping and evaluate as for a Node.js program, and through source
  maps a breakpoint in your TypeScript or framework source stops too. Pick the HTML file in the editor, a page you
  debugged before, or type a URL such as your dev server's `localhost:5173`. F5 on an HTML file serves its folder the
  way the live preview does and opens it, and an HTML file now takes breakpoints in its inline scripts. *Attach to
  Browser…* (and Debug ▸ Attach on an HTML file) attaches to a Chrome or Edge started with
  `--remote-debugging-port=9222`. launch.json `chrome` and `msedge` configurations work too. The browser runs with a
  profile of Editora's own, kept between sessions, so your everyday profile is left alone; Stop closes it. Choose
  the browser under Settings → Debugging → JavaScript. The browser has 30 seconds to start (a launch.json
  configuration's own `timeout` decides otherwise); when the debugger gives up on it, or it exits while starting,
  the status line says so and the Debug console has the debugger's own error.
- **Mark Object.** Right-click a variable, watch or result that shows an object and choose *Mark Object…* to give
  it a label, as in IntelliJ. The label then shows before that object's value wherever it appears in the session (in
  Variables, watches, results, the hover popup and Debug History), so you can follow one object as it moves between
  variables and collections. It works where the debugger shows an object's identity: Java objects, Python objects
  with an address, and pointers in native code. *Edit Mark…*, *Unmark Object* and *Unmark All Objects* are in the
  same menu.
- **View a string as JSON, XML or text.** *View As* on a string value opens its whole text in a read-only tab, laid
  out and highlighted as JSON or XML, or as plain text, so you can fold, search and copy it. If the text is not valid
  JSON or XML it opens as plain text, and the status line says why.
- **Debugging code that has no file.** When a JavaScript or TypeScript program stops or steps into code the debugger
  holds only in memory, such as code run through `eval`, that code now opens in a read-only tab with the current line
  marked, as VS Code shows it. Before, Editora said there was no source. The tab is opened once per session and shown
  again at the next stop there. You can set breakpoints in it too; they last for that debug session. Pausing a program
  that waits in a timer still shows your own line.
- **Review a branch on the Project Map.** The Changes card's *Against* menu now shows what your branch changes
  since it left the default branch, or any other branch, committed or not, as a pull request does. The branch's
  changed files get a stripe on the Map, and the folders holding them a muted one. *Compare with base* opens the
  editor's diff of a file against that commit. In every mode the card marks the words a changed line changes.
- **The Project Map follows the debugger.** When a debug session pauses, the Map opens the card of the method it
  stopped in, marks the line with the editor's amber execution line and arrow (red on an exception), and shows the
  call stack beside it. Click a frame there, or press Enter, to show it in the debugger; the card follows. Each step
  replaces the stop card where it stood, the way search hits do, unless you pinned, moved or resized it. The Map pans
  to the card but leaves the keyboard where it is. Turn it off with ⋯ → *Follow the debugger*; the Map remembers the
  choice per workspace.
- **Project Map cards have the editor's gutter.** Beside each line number a code card now shows the line's
  breakpoint, bookmark and Git change bar, and a ▶ on a JUnit test or a Java `main` method that runs it, as the
  editor's gutter does. Click in the breakpoint column to set or remove a breakpoint, in a file you have open or not;
  a running debug session is told at once. Each column appears only when the file has something to show in it, and a
  declaration card marks the file's own lines.
- **Review changes on the Project Map.** ⋯ → *Review Changes*, or *Show Changes* on a changed file or folder, opens a
  card with every file changed against HEAD (untracked ones too) and the picked file's diff, its lines numbered as in
  the old and new file. F7 / Shift+F7, the arrows, or the editor's Next / Previous Change keys on the Map step through
  the hunks of every file. Enter on a line opens that file's card at it, Ctrl+Enter the editor, and *Compare with
  HEAD* the side-by-side diff. The card follows the Git status as you save and commit.
- **Loaded Sources and Modules.** While debugging, *Debug: Loaded Sources…* lists the scripts and source files the
  program has loaded, as VS Code's Loaded Scripts does, with your project's files first. Choose one to open it: a file
  opens in its tab, ready for breakpoints, and code the debugger has only in memory (Node.js internals, code run
  through `eval`) opens read-only with the text the debugger gives. *Debug: Modules…* lists the libraries, assemblies
  or modules loaded, as Visual Studio's Modules window does, with whether their symbols are loaded; Enter copies a
  module's path. JavaScript and TypeScript list sources; Rust, C, C++, C# and Python list modules (Python lists the
  modules whose code has run). Both are in the Run menu.
- **Dependencies of the selection on the Project Map.** With ⋯ *Show dependencies of the selection* on, selecting
  a file or folder tints the rows it uses (violet), the rows that use it (olive) and the rows on both sides (amber),
  folders included, so a collapsed folder still shows that something in it is involved. The tooltip says which side
  a row is on, and the status line how many files each way. It reads the same imports as the Dependencies card, in
  the same 13 languages, and is remembered per workspace (workspace schema 34).
- **Breakpoint groups.** Put breakpoints in named groups, as in IntelliJ, and turn a whole group on or off at once:
  *Debug: Move Breakpoint to Group…* (editor menu, gutter menu, Run menu) or the breakpoint form's new *Group* field
  sets a breakpoint's group, and *Debug: Enable / Disable Breakpoint Group…* turns every breakpoint of a group on, or
  off when they all are. Method breakpoints and field watchpoints, and breakpoints in files that are not open, can be
  in a group too. In the Breakpoints list, each row names its group, typing a group's name lists its breakpoints, and
  Alt+G turns the highlighted row's group on or off.
- **Export and import breakpoints.** *Debug: Export Breakpoints…* writes every breakpoint, or one group's, to a file
  you can keep or share, with conditions, log messages, hit counts, groups and the breakpoints they wait for; files
  inside the project are written relative to it. *Debug: Import Breakpoints…* sets a file's breakpoints again, each on
  the line its code is on now, leaving lines that already have one, and a running debug session gets them at once.
  Saved with the breakpoint (`breakpoints.json` schema 9).
- **Triggered breakpoints.** A breakpoint can wait until another breakpoint is hit, as VS Code's triggered
  breakpoints and IntelliJ's "Disable until hitting the following breakpoint" do: until then it does not stop, and
  from then on it stops like any other, for the rest of that debug session. The next session it waits again. Choose
  the breakpoint to wait for with *Debug: Add Triggered Breakpoint…* (editor menu, gutter menu, Run menu, palette) or
  the *Wait for* field of the breakpoint form. In the gutter it carries an hourglass, and while it waits it is drawn
  hollow, saying which breakpoint it waits for. It works with every debugger Editora runs, in files that are not open
  too, and a breakpoint whose trigger is removed simply stops. Saved with the breakpoint (`breakpoints.json`
  schema 8).
- **Add Logpoint in one step.** Shift+click the breakpoint gutter on a line, as in IntelliJ, or use *Debug: Add
  Logpoint…* (in the editor's right-click *Breakpoints* submenu, the Run menu and the palette; `C-c C-d g` in the
  Emacs keymap). It asks only for the message to log, with `{expression}` for a value. OK makes the line a logpoint,
  which logs each time the line runs and never suspends. On a line that already has a breakpoint it edits that
  one's message and keeps its condition and hit count. Before, a logpoint took the full *Edit Breakpoint* form.
- **Lambda breakpoints in JavaScript and TypeScript.** *Debug: Toggle Lambda Breakpoint* now works on arrow
  functions and inline function expressions too: the breakpoint stops inside the function each time its body runs,
  not once when the line runs. Pick which functions of the line it stops in from the breakpoint's gutter menu, as in
  Java.
- **Problems on the Project Map.** Files with errors or warnings, and the folders that hold them, are marked on the
  Map with a red or amber dot and coloured names, and their tooltip says how many. A new *Problems* chip highlights
  them, and Next/Previous Problem on the Map steps through the whole project's problems, opening each one's card.
- **Evaluate expressions as IntelliJ does.** The Debug window has an evaluate field at the top of Variables. Its result
  is the first row, and an object's fields open under it, with Copy Value, Set Value and Add to Watches on them. A
  button beside the field adds the expression to Watches. *Debug: Evaluate Expression* (Alt+F8 in the IntelliJ keymap,
  `C-c C-d x` in Emacs, and in the editor's right-click menu while paused) now opens an Evaluate window, which you can
  keep beside the editor or open several of. It starts with the selection or the expression at the caret, and its
  result is a tree too. Both fields are small code editors: highlighted in the language you are stopped in, with your
  keymap's keys (Emacs `C-a`, `M-f`, `C-k`, `C-y`…), completion and a history kept between sessions (Up / Down,
  `M-p` / `M-n`). Shift+Enter turns a field into a code fragment of several lines, evaluated with Ctrl+Enter.
  **Alt+click** on an expression while paused evaluates it at once, a method call with its arguments included, or the
  selection when you click in it. Watches can be paused (listed but not evaluated at each stop), evaluated once, and
  removed all at once. The Debug console's input field also takes your keymap's keys now. *Debug: Focus Evaluate
  Field* goes to the field in Variables, which *Debug: Evaluate Expression* used to do for the console's field.
- **Project Map cards read like the editor.** Code cards now show the language server's semantic highlighting and
  inlay hints, and pin the headers of the class or method you have scrolled into, as the editor does. Each follows
  its editor setting.
- **Right-click menus show keybindings.** An item that does what a command does now shows that command's shortcut
  at its right edge, in the same small periwinkle type as the menu bar: the editor menu (Run, the LSP, Markdown
  and Typst submenus, the debugger items, Toggle Comment, Cut/Copy/Paste, Undo/Redo, Select All, bookmarks and
  notes), the editor tab menu, the preview menus and the Copy/Select All of the output consoles. Chords come from
  the active keymap, Emacs sequences such as `C-x C-s` included, and follow a keymap switch on the next right-click.
- **Debug Python subprocesses.** A process your Python program starts (`multiprocessing`, a Python subprocess) is now
  debugged too, in a session of its own beside the program's. Its breakpoints stop, and the Debug window shows it
  when it stops. Stopping the program stops its subprocesses, and a subprocess's tab goes once it ends. Turn it off
  with *Settings → Debugging → Python → Debug Python subprocesses*; they then run without the debugger, as before.
- **Symbol Graph on the Project Map.** *Symbol Graph* in a code card's or a declaration's menu opens a card with the
  method or class in the middle: what calls it on the left, what it calls on the right, the types it extends or
  implements above, and those that extend or implement it below. Enter on any of them moves the graph there, so you
  can walk the code; Backspace goes back. Press the middle to open its card.
- **Copy Permalink.** *Git: Copy Permalink* (in Git → History) copies the web address of the current file at the
  HEAD commit, with the selected lines (or the caret's line) marked, ready to paste in a chat or an issue. On the
  Project Map it is in a code card's menu and in a file's or folder's menu. It works with GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket,
  Gitea, Forgejo, Codeberg, sourcehut and Azure DevOps remotes, and keeps the right lines when the file has unsaved
  or uncommitted edits above them. The status bar says when HEAD is not pushed yet.
- **Debug compounds: several programs started together.** A launch.json `compounds` entry now appears in *Debug:
  Start Configuration* and starts each of its configurations in a session of its own, in order. Its `preLaunchTask`
  runs first, and with `stopAll`, stopping one stops them all. A project can also have compounds of its own saved run
  configurations: make them in *Debug: Edit Compounds…* and start them with *Debug: Start Compound…*. A launch.json
  configuration started while a session runs is now debugged beside it, as in VS Code, instead of replacing it.
- **Switch between Project Map cards by name.** On the Map, the Recent Files key (Ctrl+E in the IntelliJ keymap,
  Ctrl+R in VS Code's) or ⋯ → *Open cards* → *Switch Card…* lists the open cards, the most recently used first,
  starting on the one you were in before. Type to filter, Enter to go there.
- **Code metrics and hotspots on the Project Map.** *Code Metrics* in a folder's menu on the Map, or *Project Code
  Metrics* in the ⋯ menu, opens a card listing the folder's files, or its subfolders added up, with their lines of
  code and comments, their complexity and their commits of the last 90 days. A hotspot score marks code that is both
  complex and often changed, the hottest first; any column sorts. The summary gives the folder's totals and its code
  by language. Enter opens a file's card or looks inside a subfolder.
- **Debug several programs at once.** Start debugging another file while a session runs (F5 or *Debug File*) and
  Editora asks whether to *Debug Both*, *Stop and Debug* the new file instead, or cancel. Each session gets a tab in
  the Debug window with its own console, call stack, variables and Debug History. The toolbar, F-keys, the
  execution line, inline values and hovers follow the session shown, and a session that stops is shown by itself.
  Breakpoints, Mute and exception settings apply to every session. *Stop All* (in the tab strip, the Run menu and
  *Debug: Stop All Sessions*) ends them all. An ended session keeps its tab and output until you close it.
- **Dependencies on the Project Map.** *Dependencies* in a folder's or source file's menu on the Map, or in a code
  card's menu, and *Project Dependencies* in the ⋯ menu open a card that shows what a file or folder uses of the
  project and what uses it, file by file or folder by folder, with what is on both sides marked. For a folder,
  *Inside* shows how its parts use each other as a matrix ordered so that cycles stand out. Press anything to see the
  import lines behind it and open them; Enter moves the card onto it, and Backspace goes back. It reads the files'
  imports in Java, Kotlin, Groovy, Scala, C#, PHP, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C, C++, Ruby and Dart,
  without a build or a language server.
- **Move between Project Map cards with the keyboard.** Ctrl+Shift+arrows move the keyboard to the nearest card in
  that direction, from a card or from the map's selected row. The map only moves when that card is partly out of
  view.
- **A declaration's history as a card on the Project Map.** *Declaration History* in a declaration card's menu, or
  in a Structure row's, opens a card beside it that lists every commit that changed that method, class or field,
  newest first. Under the list, *Changes* shows what the picked commit changed in it, and *Blame* shows who last
  changed each of its lines. Enter or a double click opens the commit's diff of the file in the editor.
- **Recording breakpoints.** A breakpoint can record instead of stopping: each time it is hit, Debug History keeps the
  stop (the call stack, the frame's values, your watches) and the program goes on, without the editor jumping to it.
  Back, Forward and *Show Value History* then read the recorded stops as any other. Set one with *Debug: Toggle
  Recording Breakpoint* or *Record and continue* in the breakpoint's form; it is purple with a ring in the gutter. A
  session records at most 500 stops, after which the breakpoint stops as usual.
- **Usage counts on Project Map declaration rows.** A method, class or field row in the Map's Structure columns and a
  card's says how many times it is used ("12 uses", "no uses"), as the editor's code lens does. The counts come
  from the language server already running for the file, and update a moment after you stop typing.
- **Debug History: go back to an earlier stop.** The Debug window keeps each stop of a session as it was: the call
  stack, the values you looked at, your watches, inline values and pinned values. Back and Forward in the Debug
  toolbar (or *Debug: Back*, *Debug: Forward* and *Debug: Show History…*) show an earlier stop read-only, with its
  line marked grey in the editor and the values that changed since the stop before marked as usual. *Show Value
  History* on a variable lists its value at every stop and goes back to the one you pick. The stops are kept in
  memory only (200 by default, *Settings → Debugging → History*), and after the session ends you can still read them
  until the next one starts. Values nobody opened at a stop were never fetched, so they cannot be shown later.
- **Search the text of files on the Project Map.** Start the Map's search with `%` (`%needle`) to find text in the
  files instead of their names. The files that hold it stand out on the map. Each step through the lines found opens
  the card of the declaration that holds the line, with the text selected. That card is replaced by the next one
  unless you keep it with Ctrl+Enter, move it or pin it. *Find in Folder…* on a folder in the Map, and Find in Files
  typed in the Map window, start the same search, limited to that folder.
- **Project Map working sets keep each card's answers and caret.** References, Callers, Go to Definition and the
  other answers asked from a card come back with their edges and their "+N more" list, without asking the language
  server again. Each card comes back with its caret and scroll position. This holds for working sets and for the
  Map you see again after a restart.
- **Debug C#, Ruby and PHP.** F5 now debugs these three languages, each with its own card under *Settings →
  Debugging*, where *Install…* fetches its debugger:
  - **C#** runs on netcoredbg. Editora builds the project with `dotnet build` in the Debug console, then stops at your
    breakpoints. A lone `.cs` file works too, as a .NET 10 file-based app. An exception your code does not handle
    stops it, as in Visual Studio.
  - **Ruby** runs under rdbg, the debugger Ruby 3.1 and later ship.
  - **PHP** runs with Xdebug, through the PHP Debug adapter VS Code uses. PHP needs the Xdebug extension, and the
    adapter runs on Node.js.
  - **launch.json:** *Debug: Start Configuration…* also runs `coreclr`, `rdbg` (including attaching to
    `rdbg --open`) and `php` configurations.
  - **Samples:** `samples/debug/csharp`, `samples/debug/ruby` and `samples/debug/php`, the same shelf as the other
    languages' samples.
- **Problems on Project Map cards.** A code card underlines its file's errors and warnings as the editor does, while
  a language server runs for the file, and its status counts them. A declaration card shows only its declaration's.
  Next Problem and Previous Problem typed in a card go through the card's problems. Resting the mouse on a card's text
  shows the problems there and, on a name, its documentation.
- **Run VS Code's launch.json configurations.** *Debug: Start Configuration…* lists the configurations of the
  project's `.vscode/launch.json` and starts the one you pick as VS Code would:
  - **Supported types:** `lldb` (with its `cargo` build), `gdb`, `cppdbg`, `go` (with `exec` for a binary you built),
    `debugpy`, `node` and `java`.
  - **Variables:** VS Code's variables (`${workspaceFolder}`, `${file}`, `${env:…}` and the rest) are filled in.
    Its `inputs` ask for their values.
  - **`preLaunchTask`:** a shell or process command from `tasks.json` runs first.
  - **Remembered:** the configuration you started last is listed first.
- **GDB as the C and C++ debugger.** *Settings → Debugging → Rust, C and C++* can switch C and C++ from CodeLLDB to
  GDB, using GDB's own debug-adapter mode (GDB 14 or later).
- **Debug adapters of your own.** *Debug: Edit Debug Adapters* opens `debug-adapters.json`, where any program that
  speaks the Debug Adapter Protocol can be declared: lldb-dap, netcoredbg, a language's own. Give its command, how it
  talks, the file types it debugs, and what F5 sends it. A launch.json configuration can use it by its type, and a
  trusted project can bring its own in `.editora/debug-adapters.json`.
- **A terminal can be an editor tab.** Move to Editor, in a terminal tab's menu or the palette (Terminal: Move to
  Editor, also in the Window menu), shows the terminal as an editor tab beside your files, as IntelliJ's terminal
  does; its shell keeps running and keeps what it printed. The editor tab's menu renames it, closes it or puts it back
  with Move to Terminal Tool Window. Closing it asks first when its shell is running something, as in the tool window,
  and a window close lists it with the others. With no terminal open, Move to Editor opens a new one in the editor.
- **See every reference on the Project Map as a list.** Show References, Callers, Implementations or Subtypes as
  Cards opens six cards; the "+N more" chip used to list the rest by name only. It now opens a list beside the card
  with every place, grouped by file, each with its line's text. Type to filter by file or text, and clear *Tests* to
  leave out test files. Enter or a double-click opens a place as a card at that very line.
- **Disassembly and Memory views.** For C, C++, Rust and Go, the Debug window's third area now has *Disassembly* and
  *Memory* beside the *Console*, as VS Code, Visual Studio and IntelliJ have:
  - **Disassembly** shows the machine instructions around the selected frame, marks the one it is at, and labels each
    run of instructions with its source line; double-click one to open that line.
  - **Instruction steps:** while the Disassembly list has the keyboard, Step Over and Step Into step one instruction
    at a time. *Debug: Step Over Instruction* and *Step Into Instruction* do it from anywhere.
  - **Memory** shows the program's memory as hex and text, 256 bytes at a time, from an address or an expression.
    *View Memory* in a variable's menu opens it at that variable.
- **Following code on the Project Map no longer piles up cards.** Like an editor's preview tab, a card opened by Go
  to Definition (or Declaration, Type Definition, Super Method) is a preview, with its title in italics. The next Go
  to from it opens where it stood and replaces it, so a chain of steps keeps one card in view. Pin, drag or resize a
  preview to keep it. Back now reopens a card that was closed, at the line you were on, instead of only selecting
  its row.
- **Debug C and C++ programs.** Editora now debugs C and C++ with CodeLLDB, the debugger it already uses for Rust:
  - **F5 in a CMake project** configures a Debug build in `build/editora-debug`, builds it in the Debug console,
    and debugs the program that holds the file.
  - **F5 in a Make project** runs `make` and debugs the program it built.
  - **F5 on a file outside a project** compiles it with `cc` or `c++ -g -O0`.
  - **Trust:** CMake and Make run the project's code, so Editora asks to trust the folder first, as Maven and Cargo
    do.
  - **Values:** `std::string`, `std::vector` and `std::map` read as values.
  - **A thrown C++ exception** stops the program where it was thrown.
  - **Attach to Process** lists running Rust, C and C++ programs built with debug information, on Linux, and
    attaches CodeLLDB by process id.
  - **Settings:** *Settings → Debugging → Rust, C and C++* has a switch for C and C++.
- **Follow the code into libraries on the Project Map.** Go to Definition, callers, supertypes and the other Map
  navigation that lands in the JDK or a dependency now opens that class's source as a card, as the editor's library
  tabs do, instead of only a status note. The card is highlighted, outlined and searchable like any other, and says
  it is library source. Its Open opens the editor's library tab of that class.
- **Call and type hierarchies as trees on the Project Map.** Call Hierarchy and Type Hierarchy, typed in a Map card
  or on a declaration row, now open a tree beside the card instead of one level of cards. The tree starts with the
  callers (or, for a type, its subtypes); open a row to see its own callers, one level at a time, as deep as you
  want. It works with a language server and, for callers, without one by matching names. A function that calls
  itself through others is marked as recursive instead of repeating forever. The ⇄ button turns the tree the other
  way (callers ⇄ callees, subtypes ⇄ supertypes). Enter or a double-click opens that row's declaration as a card,
  and Back returns to where you were; Escape closes the tree. Card and declaration-row menus have *Show Call
  Hierarchy* and *Show Type Hierarchy*; *Show Callers as Cards* and the other card items are unchanged.
- **Debug Rust programs.** Editora now debugs Rust with CodeLLDB, as VS Code does with rust-analyzer:
  - **F5 in a Cargo package**, or *Debug File* in the editor's right-click menu, builds with Cargo in the Debug
    console, then debugs the program Cargo built. In an `examples/` file it debugs that example.
  - **In a `#[test]` function**, F5 and *Debug Test at Caret* debug that test alone. Outside a test, an
    integration-test file debugs all its tests.
  - **Values** are shown as Rust values: a `String` reads as its text, and a `Vec` or a `HashMap` expands to its
    items.
  - **A panic** stops the program where it happened.
  - **Debugging features:** breakpoints (with conditions, hit counts and logpoints), stepping, Variables, Watches
    and the Threads view all work.
  - **Setup:** *Settings → Debugging → Rust* turns Rust debugging on or off, sets CodeLLDB's path, and has an
    Install button that fetches CodeLLDB's pinned release and checks its checksum. A CodeLLDB already installed in
    VS Code is found too. The Doctor checks for it.
- **Debug Go programs.** Editora now debugs Go with Delve, as VS Code's Go extension does:
  - **F5 on a Go file**, or *Debug File* in the editor's right-click menu, debugs its package, or the file alone
    outside a module.
  - **In a `_test.go` file**, F5 and *Debug Test at Caret* run the test function the caret is in (a benchmark on
    its own), or every test of the package.
  - **Attach to Process** lists running Go programs and attaches by process id. *Stop* leaves the program running.
  - **Debugging features:** breakpoints (with conditions, hit counts and logpoints), stepping, Variables, Watches,
    inline values and the Threads view all work. Goroutines are listed as threads.
  - **Setup:** Delve is found on the PATH or where `go install` puts it. *Settings → Debugging → Go* turns Go
    debugging on or off, sets Delve's path, and installs Delve with `go install`. The Doctor checks for it.
  - **Build output:** Delve's build goes to the temporary folder, not your package.
- **One Back and Forward on the Project Map.** The Map kept two histories: Alt+Left / Alt+Right and the ‹ ›
  buttons went back through the rows you visited, while Back typed in a card went back through the cards you followed
  the code through, and neither knew about the other. Now both are one history. Back and Forward on the map, typed in
  a card, or picked from the buttons' menu go through the rows you visited and the cards you followed in the order you
  visited them. A card comes back with its caret where you left it. If you closed the card since, Back goes to its row
  instead of skipping it. The menu says which line each card stop was at, and Back and Forward typed anywhere on the
  Map now stay on the Map instead of moving the editor.
- **Move around inside a Project Map card.** Go to Line, the matching bracket and Beginning / End of Defun, typed in
  a card with your keymap's keys, now move the card's caret instead of the editor's. Go to Line opens a small bar
  under the card's title, numbered as the file numbers its lines, so a declaration card's lines keep their file
  numbers. In a file card, Alt+Page Up and Alt+Page Down move the caret to the declaration before or after it, as they
  already step a declaration card through its file. The card menu has *Go to Line…* and, in a file card, *Previous
  Declaration* and *Next Declaration*. When the caret rests on a name, its other uses in the card are highlighted, as
  in the editor.
- **See what a function calls on the Project Map.** *Show Callees as Cards*, in a Map card's menu and a declaration
  row's, opens a card for each declaration the function calls, joined to it by a "calls" edge with the number of call
  sites. It asks the language server's call hierarchy for outgoing calls, the counterpart of *Show Callers as Cards*.
  Calls to code already in the card open no card. It's also a command, *Project Map: Show Callees as Cards*, which you
  can bind to a key.
- **Go to File and Go to Symbol open cards on the Project Map.** Typed in the Map window, the file finder (Ctrl+P in
  VS Code, Ctrl+Shift+N in IntelliJ, `C-x C-f` in Emacs) and Go to Symbol in Workspace now open over the Map, and what
  you pick opens as a card there, its name selected, instead of an editor tab. The finder starts in the folder of the
  card you're in, Go to Symbol asks that card's language server, and Back returns to the card you came from. Without a
  language server, Go to Symbol starts an `@name` search in the Map instead.
- **Method breakpoints and field watchpoints show in the gutter.** They were listed only in *Debug: Breakpoints*.
  Each is now marked on its member's declaration line in an open Java file — every overload of a method — as
  IntelliJ and Eclipse do: a dot with an arrow into it for a method breakpoint, a dot with an eye for a field
  watchpoint, gold when it has a condition and grey when disabled. Hover it to see what it is; click it to remove
  it; right-click it to disable or remove it. The mark follows its member as you edit.
- **Lambda breakpoints in Java.** A line breakpoint stops once, when its line runs, never inside a lambda on that
  line. *Debug: Toggle Lambda Breakpoint* (Shift+F9 in the VS Code, CUA and Sublime keymaps) sets one that stops
  inside the lambda at the caret each time its body runs, with the lambda's parameters in Variables, as VS Code's
  inline breakpoints and IntelliJ's lambda breakpoints do. Right-click a breakpoint's dot on a line with lambdas to
  choose where it stops: **Stop on the Line**, and **Stop in Lambda 1**, **2**… for each lambda the line starts.
  Such a breakpoint carries a λ on its dot, keeps its condition, hit count and log message for every place it stops,
  and is saved with the project's breakpoints.
- **Navigate code on the Project Map.** The editor's code navigation now works inside Map cards and answers with
  cards beside them instead of leaving the Map: Go to Definition (and Peek Definition), Go to Declaration, Go to Type
  Definition, Go to Implementation, Go to Super Method, Find Usages, Call Hierarchy and Type Hierarchy, typed with
  your keymap's keys or picked from a card's menu, and Ctrl+click (Cmd+click on macOS) on a name. Each result card is
  joined to the card it came from by a labelled edge ("definition", "implements", "extends"…), the keyboard follows a
  definition to its card, and Back and Forward step between the cards you followed. Quick Documentation shows the
  language server's hover over a card. Without a language server, Go to Definition finds the declarations of that
  name. A declaration row's menu offers the same, and a card menu's **In the Editor** submenu still runs these
  commands in the editor.
- **Pinned values while debugging.** *Debug: Pin Value to Line* pins the selection, or the expression at the caret,
  to the caret's line (or asks for one), as Visual Studio's pinned DataTips and IntelliJ's inline watches do: at
  every stop it is evaluated in the selected frame and its value painted at the end of that line, after the values
  the editor shows by itself — `total = 3  ·  items.size() = 2`. **Pin to Line** in the hover's value popup does the
  same. Pins follow their line through edits, are saved with the project's breakpoints, and *Debug: Unpin Values on
  Line* removes them; running the same command again unpins one.
- **Attach to Process.** *Debug: Attach to Process…* (Run menu, and the last row of the Attach picker) lists the
  Java, Node.js and Python programs running on this machine — those listening for a debugger first: a JVM started
  with the JDWP agent (`-agentlib:jdwp=…,server=y,address=5005`), a Node.js started with `--inspect`, a Python
  under `python -m debugpy --listen` (or `python …/debugpy --listen`; debugpy's own adapter and launcher processes
  are left out). Picking one attaches the right debugger; Stop detaches and the program runs on. A program started
  without debugging says what to start it with. **Python programs can now be attached to** (debugpy's `--listen`),
  and a Java attach is remembered for *Debug: Reattach*.
- **Exception card.** When the program stops on an exception, a card opens under the line that threw it, as
  Visual Studio's Exception Helper and VS Code's exception widget do: whether the program catches it, its type and
  message, the exceptions that caused it and the stack trace when the debugger sends them (Python and
  JavaScript), with **Copy** and — for a caught exception — **Don’t Stop on Caught Exceptions**. It never takes
  focus: Esc in the editor or a click elsewhere closes it, and Continue, a step or another frame does too.
  *Debug: Show Exception* opens it again.
- **JSON Lines files.** `.jsonl`, `.ndjson` and `.jsonlines` files open as **JSON Lines**: each line is coloured as
  JSON, a line that is not exactly one JSON value (a trailing comma, two records on one line, a record split over
  two lines) is underlined with what is wrong, and the preview shows the records as a tree keyed by line number —
  or, when a line is broken, a link to it. JSON Lines is in **File ▸ New**, spell check skips it like JSON, a
  `jsonl` Markdown fence is coloured, and an HTTP response sent as `application/x-ndjson` is saved as `.jsonl`.
- **Threads view.** The Debug window's Call Stack area has a **Threads** switch (and *Debug: Threads* opens it):
  every thread of the program, which are suspended and why, and which is shown. Right-click a thread to **Pause
  Thread** or **Resume Thread** — that thread alone, the others staying as they are — or **Show Frames** of a
  suspended one (also Enter or a double-click). Threads starting and ending update the list.
- **Show numbers as hexadecimal while debugging.** *Debug: Show Numbers as Hexadecimal* (also in the Variables
  context menu) shows integer values in hexadecimal in Variables, watches, hover and inline values, through the debug
  protocol's `format.hex` (Java and Python honour it).
- **Filter the Variables tree.** A filter field beside the Variables heading narrows each scope to the variables whose
  name contains what you type; Esc clears it, Down moves into the tree. Watches are left alone.
- **Go to Index in a long collection.** A list or array with more than 100 elements, once opened, has **Go to
  Index…** in its context menu: its elements are shown from that index, 100 at a time as before.
- **Force Run to Cursor.** Runs to the caret line with every breakpoint on the way ignored (IntelliJ keymap
  Ctrl+Alt+F9, Emacs `C-c C-d S-u`, the Run ▸ Debugger menu and the editor menu while paused). Exception
  breakpoints still stop the program, and the breakpoints are back at the next stop.
- **Attach remembers where it attached.** Debug ▸ Attach to Running Program offers this project's last eight
  addresses, most recent first, with "Another address…" last; *Debug: Reattach* attaches again to the last one
  without asking (Emacs `C-c C-d S-a`).
- **`.env` files in run configurations.** In a configuration's Environment field, an entry `@.env` (or any path,
  quoted when it has spaces) loads that file — relative to the working directory — where it stands: later
  `NAME=value` entries override it and can use its variables. A file that cannot be read stops the launch and says
  which. Works for Run and Debug.
- **Changed values are highlighted after a step.** In the Debug window's Variables tree, a value that differs from
  what the same frame showed at the previous stop is tinted and bold, as in VS Code, Visual Studio, Eclipse, NetBeans
  and IntelliJ. A new variable is not marked, and a new session starts with nothing to compare.
- **Temporary breakpoints.** *Debug: Toggle Temporary Breakpoint* (IntelliJ keymap Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F8, Emacs
  `C-c C-d 1`, the Run ▸ Debugger menu and the editor menu) sets a breakpoint that is removed once the program stops
  on it; the Edit Breakpoint form has **Remove once hit**. Its gutter dot carries a "1".
- **Copy Call Stack.** The Call Stack's context menu (and Ctrl+C in the list) copies the stopped thread's whole
  stack, folded runtime frames included, as `at name(File.java:12)` lines.
- **Method breakpoints and field watchpoints (Java).** *Debug: Toggle Method Breakpoint* stops the program when the
  method the caret is in is entered; *Debug: Toggle Field Watchpoint* stops it when the field declared on the caret
  line is assigned (Emacs `C-c C-d S-m` and `C-c C-d S-w`, and the Run ▸ Debugger menu). Away from a method or field
  they ask for one by name, such as `com.example.Order#total`. While paused, **Break When Value Changes** in the
  Variables menu watches the field a row shows. They are saved with the project's breakpoints, listed in
  *Debug: Breakpoints* (enable, disable, remove, jump), muted with the others, and the state line says which stopped
  the program.
- **Suspend all threads when one stops** (Settings → Debugging, Java, off by default): a breakpoint, exception or
  step stops every thread of the program, and Continue resumes them all — IntelliJ's "Suspend: All".
- **The mouse wheel zooms a PDF.** A plain wheel zooms an open PDF around the pointer (before, only Ctrl+wheel
  did), Ctrl/Cmd+wheel zooms faster and a touchpad pinch zooms too. Shift+wheel pans across, Alt+wheel pans down and
  a sideways swipe pans, as on the Project Map; dragging still pans.

### Changed

- **Internal: JavaFX 27 → 27.0.1, and RichTextFX fork 0.11.7-inlay.3.** JavaFX 27.0.1 hands the editor's own
  styled-text clipboard value back as a `ByteBuffer` (in the headless toolkit, the serialized array), where the
  fork's paste cast it to `byte[]` and threw. The fork's paste now reads either form; nothing else changed in it.
- **Long documents stay light on screen (PERF-08).** The Markdown preview builds only the blocks on and near the
  screen, so a 20,000-line document holds a screenful of blocks instead of thousands, and scrolling it does no
  work in its length; Find in the preview, selection, Copy, the outline links and the split view's scroll sync
  work as before. The fstab, systemd, ssh config, Dockerfile, GitHub Actions and OpenAPI previews, the HTTP
  client's request list and the newer-versions dialog are scrolling lists that build only the rows shown; the pom
  preview, the merge view (20 conflicts a page), Parallel Stacks, the note card and a few small lists show a
  named number of items and say how many more there are. Query Replace reads only as far as the next match, and
  the CSV grid's filter, the Markdown format bar and the File Information panel no longer read the whole file
  on each key.
- **Typing, pickers and editor commands no longer pause on large files and projects.** The work behind them now runs
  in the background and lands a moment later:
  - typing in Search Everywhere, the command palette, every picker, Find File, the Settings search and the Git log,
    Structure, TODO, Bookmarks, Notes and Build Actions filters (an Enter pressed meanwhile acts on the latest
    results), and the status bar's word count;
  - typing in a file synced to a language server (the change is worked out as it is sent, in order);
  - Enter, Backspace and the list, heading, link, table-of-contents and format commands in long Markdown documents,
    and the heading crumbs;
  - the console find bar (the count appears once you pause typing);
  - Select All Occurrences, matching-bracket jumps, Expand Selection, Query Replace, Toggle Comment, tag
    auto-rename, CSV Align, Convert Indentation and whole-file replacements;
  - folding, hover and documentation popups (a long doc may show as plain text for a moment), the merge resolver's
    Save, the Map's Changes card (changed words are marked just after the lines show), breakpoints moved by
    edits during a debug session;
  - math in the Markdown preview, popups and the agent panel (a new formula appears a moment after its text),
    Copy HTML, the debug expression field's colours and the status bar's size.
  Two small differences: Ctrl/Cmd-click on a Markdown link now also moves the caret there, and a `*/` more than
  4,096 characters below no longer stops `/**` from closing itself. A close-save in the merge resolver closes the tab
  once the result is applied, and with `--single-window` the window appears once its session has been read.
- **Searching, matching and checking a document no longer hold up typing.** The find bar searches, and works out
  Replace and Replace All, in the background for every document, not only large ones: the matches light up a moment
  after you pause, and a Replace All with text typed meanwhile is worked out again on the new text, still as one undo
  step. The tab's modified mark is checked in the background: an undo back to the saved text of a large file clears
  the mark a moment later (it never shows "saved" for text that differs). Find in Files' Replace All on open tabs, the
  link updates in open Markdown tabs after a rename, the shell script's own names in completion, a matching bracket
  far off-screen, the ▶ marks after a file opens, the unused pasted images after a save and an HTTP request's history
  entry are all worked out in the background and shown when they land. Run, Debug, Git, Diff and the close question save in the background
  and go on once the file is written, instead of holding the window meanwhile (Save in the close question closes the
  tab when the save is done); a file's personal notes and the Markdown preview's find are also worked out in the
  background; Debug Test on a Gradle project waits for its
  debug script the same way. Windows opened after the first are built without reading their layout file again.
- **Amber, red and green now mean only a warning, an error and a success.** Bookmarks, Personal Notes, the Stop
  buttons, deleted lines and the Map's recent-changes heat no longer borrow them. A bookmark and a note are the
  accent, in the gutter, the Project tree and the editor's note wash, told apart by their shapes, and the code-action
  bulb is the muted ink (red still marks a quick fix for an error). A note's popup, its Map card and its sticky notes
  are an accent wash on the theme's own ground instead of yellow paper. Stop (the toolbar's run cluster, a running
  `.http` request's ■ and the other Stop glyphs) is drawn in the ink. Deleted and removed lines are neutral grey in
  the diff viewer, the change bar's wedge, a change's popup, the Git counts, a pull request, a patch and Git's output,
  and changed lines are blue. The debugger's execution line, its arrow, the current disassembly row and the Map's stop
  card are the accent (IntelliJ's execution point), conditional and recording breakpoints are red like the others,
  and a logpoint is the accent. The Map's heat, its metrics table's heat and Find in the Markdown preview are the
  accent, a Markdown TIP alert is grey, OpenAPI method badges are one accent, a JSON or XML preview's strings and
  literals and a log's INFO lines follow the theme without the state colours, and the dev-mode badge is the accent.
  In the editor, a search match, an assigned symbol's highlight and a jump label are the accent instead of yellow,
  orange and peach, and the minimap marks deleted lines in grey. The Git log's graph lanes and a Markwhen timeline's
  tags take six blue-to-magenta hues of the theme, none of them red, green or amber. Everything drawn on a canvas
  (the editor's overlays and stripes, the minimap, the Git log graph, the diff's overview, the Project Map) now takes
  its colours from the app theme, so it follows a theme switch.
  A deprecated OpenAPI operation is amber (a warning) rather than red. Read-only View Mode's banner follows the theme's
  amber. Pauta 6.0.1: ICON-07, ICON-08, ICON-09, ICON-18.
- **A few hints read better.** An unresolved Maven version, the "locked" hint of an encrypted file, a Thread Dump
  frame with no source, a log's TRACE lines and the line numbers of the default Primer Light editor theme and the
  community themes' editor were drawn in the faintest text colour; they now use the muted one, 4.5:1 or more
  (ICON-09).
- **Print Preview follows the interface zoom.** Its bar's text, buttons and gaps, and the window's size, grow and
  shrink with the interface zoom (View: Zoom In Interface) like every other window (WIN-12, Pauta 6.0.1), and a
  change of the zoom reaches an open preview at once. The page at "100%" is drawn as large as the text around it;
  Fit Page and Fit Width still fill the window. The page itself keeps the size it was laid out at, and prints
